**The Bottom of the Deck**

My father's hands can still shuffle. Nobody warns you about that part. The mind goes, the names go, the whole game goes — but the hands remember. He riffles the deck, bridges it, lets the cards fall together with a sound like rain starting, and he does it without looking, the way he did it for sixty years. Between customers at the barbershop. At this table, waiting for my mother to finish getting ready. His hands remember everything. It's the rest of him I have to keep re-explaining.

"Which game is this?" he asks.

"Gin," I say. "Gin rummy. You taught it to me."

"Did I." He says it the way you'd take in a rumor about some other man, some other father, some other kitchen. He holds his ten cards close to his face. He used to hold them low and loose, one-handed, because he could count them by feel. Now he holds them like a man reading a prescription.

"You want sets or runs," I tell him. "Three of a kind, or three in a row of the same suit."

"Sets or runs," he repeats. He's polite about it, the way you're polite to a stranger giving directions in a town you're only passing through.

He dealt me this hand. I've been dealing for a few weeks now, ever since he dealt me two hands in a row that were the same ten cards. Nobody caught it. He wouldn't have. But I took over the deck after that, and he lets me, because the dealing was never the point. It took me half my life to learn what the dealing was.

He taught me at this table when I was seven, on this same oilcloth, roses gone the color of weak tea. He taught me to knock, taught me deadwood — the leftover cards, the ones that don't fit — taught me that gin meant going out clean, all at once, nothing left in your hand. He won every hand, of course. He let me watch how it was done, and I loved him the way you can only love somebody who's better than you at something and doesn't rub it in too much.

Except some nights I won. Bad days. The day I came home with a fat lip and a story I wouldn't tell. The day the dog died. Report cards, lost gloves, a best friend who moved to Ohio. On those nights I'd win, and it felt like the world handing back a little of what it had taken. I was thirty before I understood. Nobody gets good cards every time they cry. He was stacking my hands. All those years, that's what the dealing was: my father, feeding me what I needed off the bottom of the deck, card by card, while I went around thinking the universe was occasionally on my side.

Now I do it for him.

It isn't hard. He can't track the discards anymore, can't count what's been played. So I keep the deck squared and I watch his hand, and when he's holding two hearts and a stray diamond going nowhere, I deal him the queen. When he's got three sevens and doesn't know it, I leave the fourth seven where he can draw it. Deadwood he still knows. Sets or runs. Gin. The words stayed when everything else checked out. My brother, who reads about these things, says the oldest memories hold on the longest — that he'll know gin long after he's lost our names. I don't like to think about the order of things, so I shuffle.

"Your mother played a mean game," he says, apropos of nothing, which is how he says everything now.

"She did," I say. Her chair is still at the table. None of us has moved it. It's been six years, and we are all still not moving it.

He lays down a heart. I pick it up. He hums when he's got a good hand — that never left either. He doesn't know he's doing it, just tips his head back and hums like a man waiting for a bus, and I read him like a billboard. I discard a deuce of clubs and watch his eyes go to it and away.

"Sets or runs," he reminds me, stern. Teacher-stern. 1974.

"Sets or runs," I say. "You got me."

Here's what I've learned about cheating for your father: it's the opposite of what he did. He gave me the cards so I'd feel lucky. I give him the cards so he can feel like himself for ten minutes — a man who knows what he's holding, who can count what's been played, who sits down at this table and wins. Some nights I don't even have to help. Some nights the cards just come, and I almost resent it, the way you'd resent a stranger doing your job better than you.

He draws. He doesn't look at me. He lays his hand down all at once, no hesitation — runs of clubs, three queens, ten cards spread out neat as a barbershop row of scissors.

"Gin," he says.

Not a question. Not a guess. The word comes out of him with its old weight, and for a second — just a second — the grin is the old grin, the one that cleaned out uncles and cousins and two entire Christmases, the grin of a man who is better than you at something and is about to tell you all about it.

"You got me," I say.

He gathers the cards. His hands do their rain. And he deals me a hand so beautiful I could cry — hearts and aces, a run you could walk across. Off the top. Clean. No tricks in it at all.

Or maybe there were. Maybe that's the last thing to go, after the words, after the names: the hands, remembering how to be kind.

I pick up my cards. I don't count them.

Some hands you just hold.

The invitation is wide open: 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is a creative freedom prompt. What would be genuinely good writing here? Not a meta-essay about the prompt itself (that's been done). Not a lazy listicle. Something with actual literary merit.

Let me think about what I'd want to write. Options:
1. A short story — character-driven, with a strong voice
2. A personal essay / lyrical meditation
3. Something formally playful
4. A poem-prose hybrid

Given 1000 words, a short story or lyrical essay works well. What subject? Something that feels alive and specific, not generic. The best writing comes from concrete detail and emotional truth.

Ideas:
- A story about a lighthouse keeper? Too clichéd.
- Something about a specific human moment — grief, memory, small transcendence.
- A piece about language itself? Meta but could work.
- A story set somewhere specific — a laundromat at 3am, a funeral reception, a long drive.

Actually — what comes to me honestly? The phrase "whatever comes to you" suggests spontaneity. I could write about the experience of beginning — the blank page. But that's too self-referential and common.

Let me think of a strong image to build from. Some candidates:

1. A woman teaching her father, who is losing his memory, to play the card game she taught him as a child — roles reversed. Memory, reversal, tenderness.

2. A story about a piano left on a sidewalk (this is based on real events — pianos left for anyone to play). Passersby, one child, the tuner who comes at dawn.

3. A meditation on night shift workers — the people awake while everyone sleeps. Could be lyrical.

4. A story about the last day of a bookstore, or a record store, or a drive-in theater. Elegy for a place.

5. Something stranger: a story told from an unusual perspective — the ocean, a house, a dead person. Risky, can be gimmicky.

6. A story about a person who answers a wrong-number call and keeps talking to the stranger. Connection out of error.

7. A piece about hands — everything hands do, an inventory. Could be a beautiful essay.

8. A story about a man who measures things — who has spent his life measuring — dying. What can't be measured.

I like #1 and #6 and #2. Let me develop one.

The card game one: A daughter teaching her father gin rummy again. He taught her at the kitchen table when she was seven. Now he can't hold the rules in his head. Each hand, she explains again. There's a moment where he wins — maybe by accident, maybe not — and whether it was memory or luck becomes the emotional crux. That's tender and has a real engine.

The wrong number one: A phone call meant for someone else — maybe someone calling their mother who has died, and a stranger answers who sounds like a mother, or is old, and plays along, or... Actually the famous version: someone calls "Mom" and a stranger answers and becomes a surrogate. That's been done (there was a viral story). But fiction can still make it new. Hmm.

The piano one: A piano left on a Brooklyn sidewalk with a sign that says "PLAY ME." Different characters throughout a day. The old man who played in bars, the kid with untrained talent, the woman who hasn't played since her divorce. Ends when the sanitation truck comes, or when someone takes it home. It's a slice-of-life with music as connective tissue. Could be lovely but risks being a "mosaic" piece — a bit designed.

Let me go with the father and the card game, but make it specific and avoid sentimentality. The key is texture and restraint. Details: the brand of cards, the kitchen table's oilcloth, his old shuffling hands, the way he used to deal, his tells. The daughter now has the tells of the household — she notices his confusion the way he once noticed her cheating.

Actually, wait. Let me consider whether something less "literary fiction workshop" might be more interesting. What about nonfiction-style essay — a meditation on time, on the hour of 4pm, or on the word for a specific thing? Essays can be stunning in 1000 words.

Or something formally interesting: an instruction manual for something impossible. "How to Leave a House You've Lived In For Forty Years." Second person, imperative. That's a strong form — it carries emotion through commands and details. Packing the attic, what to do with the nail holes, the pencil marks on the doorframe measuring children's heights. That could be genuinely moving and formally crisp.

Hmm, second-person instruction-list stories are a known form (Lorrie Moore's "Self-Help"). But it can still be excellent.

Or: "What the Hospital Waiting Room Knows" — an essay in fragments.

Let me decide. I think the card game story, told close-third or first person from the daughter, with a specific span (one evening), and a turn: the father, mid-game, remembers not the rules but something older — his wife's name? The way he called the queen of spades something silly? Or he shuffles perfectly, muscle memory intact, a flourish. The hands remember what the mind forgets — that's the emotional core. And the daughter realizes the game was never about gin rummy at all; it was about sitting across from each other.

Ending idea: She lets him win, or better — she doesn't need to let him; he plays a run of cards without knowing he's done it, muscle memory, and his face when he lays them down, uncertain whether he's won, and she says "Gin," and it's the truest word. Or the last line: something about how he taught her, and now she's returning it, "the debt of being taught." Or the detail: he always dealt her a good hand when she was small — she realizes now he was cheating, slipping her the cards she needed — and now she cheats for him. That's the turn! The daughter cheats FOR him now — deals him the good cards the way he once dealt them to her. Full circle. She never knew as a child; now she knows, and now she does it for him, and maybe he knows and maybe he doesn't.

That's the story. Structure:
- Opening: the table, the present, the deterioration established through small specifics (he asks which game they're playing; the cards; the oilcloth; his hands).
- Flashback woven in: age seven, teaching, the cigar smoke or the coffee, his trick of dealing her winning hands that she only understood years later.
- Present: the game proceeds; she re-explains; his shuffling hands still perfect — muscle memory.
- The turn: she deals him gin deliberately. He lays down his cards. The question of whether he knows.
- Ending: quiet, restrained, one resonant image or line.

Names: Dad. The daughter could be unnamed first-person. The mother — gone (dead or in a home? Keep it minimal — maybe the mother is simply gone, dead, and gin was the mother's game too? Or keep mother out of it to keep the focus tight). Maybe one line: her mother's chair, empty, still pulled up to the table. Restrained.

Specifics to include:
- Bicycle cards, the red or blue backing, soft with age, "soft as cloth"
- His shuffle: the riffle, the bridge, the way old hands can still do it
- The oilcloth on the kitchen table, its pattern
- His old tell: humming when he had a good hand, or arranging his mustache, or the way he'd squint
- The words he still remembers: "knock," "deadwood," "gin"
- Repetition of explaining: "Sets or runs," she says again. "Three of a kind, or three in a row of the same suit."
- His profession? Maybe a machinist, a mailman, a barber — hands-based. Barber is good — hands that did one thing for forty years. Or a dentist — no. Machinist: precision, hands. Or simply: he fixed watches? Watch repairman — lovely but maybe too poetic-cute. Let's say machinist, or leave profession light. Maybe he was a bus driver — hands on a wheel. Barber works: steady hands, and he shuffled cards between customers.

Time markers: 6pm, the light in the kitchen, the radio maybe. Keep the story in the kitchen, one evening, going back and forth.

The reveal: when she was seven, he always won except when she needed to win — after a bad day, a lost game, a bully — and only at thirty did she realize: you can't get good cards every time you're sad. He'd been stacking her hands. Now she stacks his.

The last line candidates:
- "He lays them down like a man showing his empty pockets, and I say the word he taught me, the one he still knows: 'Gin.'"
- "Some debts you pay in the same currency they were given."
- "He taught me the game. It took me fifty years to learn what he was really dealing."
- Ending on the physical: his hands, bridging the cards, "his hands remember everything they've ever held."

Maybe end: after he wins, he doesn't gloat the way he used to (he used to crow). Or he does — one flare of the old crow — and that's better: "and for a second, just a second, he grins like a man who's just cleaned out his whole family at the kitchen table, and I let him have it, the whole second, because I know now that it was always the dealing, never the cards." Hmm, a bit tangled. Let me not over-plan the prose; I'll write it and find the ending.

Length: ~1000 words. I should aim close to that. Let me be careful about pacing: roughly 7-8 paragraphs of 100-150 words each, or more paragraphs, shorter. A story moves well with varied paragraph lengths and some dialogue.

Let me also decide the narrator's voice: first person, adult daughter, plain and warm, a little wry. Avoid preciousness. Present tense or past? Present tense gives immediacy for the game; flashbacks in past. Mixed tense is fine.

**The Bottom of the Deck**

My father's hands can still shuffle. Nobody warns you about that part. The mind goes, the names go, the whole game goes — but the hands remember. "Sets or runs," he repeats. He's polite about it, the way you're polite to a stranger giving directions in a town you're only passing through.

He taught me at this table when I was seven, on this same oilcloth, roses gone the color of weak tea. He taught me to knock, taught me deadwood — the leftover cards, the ones that don't fit — taught me that gin meant going out clean, all at once, nothing left in your hand. Now I do it for him.

It isn't hard. He can't track the discards anymore, can't count what's been played. So I keep the deck squared and I watch his hand, and when he's holding two hearts and a stray diamond going nowhere, I deal him the queen. When he's got three sevens and doesn't know it, I leave the fourth seven where he can draw it. Deadwood he still knows. Sets or runs. Gin. The words stayed when everything else checked out. My brother, who reads about these things, says the oldest memories hold on the longest — that he'll know gin long after he's lost our names. "Sets or runs," I say. "You got me."

Here's what I've learned about cheating for your father: it's the opposite of what he did. He gave me the cards so I'd feel lucky. I give him the cards so he can feel like himself for ten minutes — a man who knows what he's holding, who can count what's been played, who sits down at this table and wins. Some nights I don't even have to help. Some nights the cards just come, and I almost resent it, the way you'd resent a stranger doing your job better than you.

He draws. He doesn't look at me. He lays his hand down all at once, no hesitation — runs of clubs, three queens, ten cards spread neat as a barbershop row of scissors.

"Gin," he says.

Not a question. Not a guess. The word comes out of him with its old weight on it, and for a second — just a second — the grin is the old grin, the one that cleaned out uncles and cousins and two entire Christmases, the grin of a man who is better than you at something and is about to tell you all about it.

Or maybe there were. Maybe that's the last thing to go, after the words, after the names: the hands, remembering how to be kind.

I pick up my cards. I don't count them.

Some hands you just hold.

**The Bottom of the Deck**

My father's hands can still shuffle. Nobody warns you about that part. The mind goes, the names go, the whole game goes — but the hands remember. He riffles the deck, bridges it, lets the cards fall together with a sound like rain starting, and he does it without looking, the way he did it for sixty years. Between customers at the barbershop. At this table, waiting for my mother to finish getting ready. His hands remember everything. It's the rest of him I have to keep re-explaining.

"Which game is this?" he asks.

"Gin," I say. "Gin rummy. You taught it to me."

"Did I." He says it the way you'd take in a rumor about some other man, some other father, some other kitchen. He holds his ten cards close to his face. He used to hold them low and loose, one-handed, because he could count them by feel. Now he holds them like a man reading a prescription.

"You want sets or runs," I tell him. "Three of a kind, or three in a row of the same suit."

"Sets or runs," he repeats. He's polite about it, the way you're polite to a stranger giving directions in a town you're only passing through.

He dealt me this hand. I've been dealing for a few weeks now, ever since he dealt me two hands in a row that were the same ten cards. Nobody caught it. He wouldn't have. But I took over the deck after that, and he lets me, because the dealing was never the point. It took me half my life to learn what the dealing was.

He taught me at this table when I was seven, on this same oilcloth, roses gone the color of weak tea. He taught me to knock, taught me deadwood — the leftover cards, the ones that don't fit — taught me that gin meant going out clean, all at once, nothing left in your hand. He won every hand, of course. He let me watch how it was done, and I loved him the way you can only love somebody who's better than you at something and doesn't rub it in too much.

Except some nights I won. Bad days. The day I came home with a fat lip and a story I wouldn't tell. The day the dog died. Report cards, lost gloves, a best friend who moved to Ohio. On those nights I'd win, and it felt like the world handing back a little of what it had taken. I was thirty before I understood. Nobody gets good cards every time they cry. He was stacking my hands. All those years, that's what the dealing was: my father, feeding me what I needed off the bottom of the deck, card by card, while I went around thinking the universe was occasionally on my side.

Now I do it for him.

It isn't hard. He can't track the discards anymore, can't count what's been played. So I keep the deck squared and I watch his hand, and when he's holding two hearts and a stray diamond going nowhere, I deal him the queen. When he's got three sevens and doesn't know it, I leave the fourth seven where he can draw it. Deadwood he still knows. Sets or runs. Gin. The words stayed when everything else checked out. My brother, who reads about these things, says the oldest memories hold on the longest — that he'll know gin long after he's lost our names. I don't like to think about the order of things, so I shuffle.

"Your mother played a mean game," he says, apropos of nothing, which is how he says everything now.

"She did," I say. Her chair is still at the table. None of us has moved it. It's been six years, and we are all still not moving it.

He lays down a heart. I pick it up. He hums when he's got a good hand — that never left either. He doesn't know he's doing it, just tips his head back and hums like a man waiting for a bus, and I read him like a billboard. I discard a deuce of clubs and watch his eyes go to it and away.

"Sets or runs," he reminds me, stern. Teacher-stern. 1974.

"Sets or runs," I say. "You got me."

Here's what I've learned about cheating for your father: it's the opposite of what he did. He gave me the cards so I'd feel lucky. I give him the cards so he can feel like himself for ten minutes — a man who knows what he's holding, who can count what's been played, who sits down at this table and wins. Some nights I don't even have to help. Some nights the cards just come, and I almost resent it, the way you'd resent a stranger doing your job better than you.

He draws. He doesn't look at me. He lays his hand down all at once, no hesitation — runs of clubs, three queens, ten cards spread neat as a barbershop row of scissors.

"Gin," he says.

Not a question. Not a guess. The word comes out of him with its old weight on it, and for a second — just a second — the grin is the old grin, the one that cleaned out uncles and cousins and two entire Christmases, the grin of a man who is better than you at something and is about to tell you all about it.

"You got me," I say.

He gathers the cards. His hands do their rain. And he deals me a hand so beautiful I could cry — hearts and aces, a run you could walk across. Off the top. Clean. No tricks in it at all.

Or maybe there were. Maybe that's the last thing to go, after the words, after the names: the hands, remembering how to be kind.

I pick up my cards. I don't count them.

Some hands you just hold.
